prompt: Mark and Ana married in Texas in 2015. In 2019 Mark inherited a lake lot from his aunt, and in 2020 the couple bought a house with their salaries. How is each property classified?

options.text: Both are community property, since each was acquired during marriage
The lot is Mark's separate property; the house is presumed community
The lot is community property; the house belongs to the higher earner
Both are held as tenants by the entirety, since the couple is married

explanation: Texas is a community property state. Property acquired during marriage is presumed community, owned equally by both spouses, but property owned before marriage or acquired by gift, devise, or descent is separate property. Mark's inherited lot is separate; the house bought with salaries is community. Income from separate property is generally community in Texas.

distractorExplanations.a: Inheritances are separate property even when received during marriage.
distractorExplanations.c: An inheritance stays separate, and community property is owned in equal halves, not by earnings.
distractorExplanations.d: Texas does not recognize tenancy by the entirety; marital property is classified as community or separate.

prompt: An electric cooperative holds a recorded right to run power lines across a ranch. The right does not benefit any neighboring parcel. What type of interest is this?

options.text: An easement appurtenant that benefits a dominant tenement
A license, a personal permission the ranch owner may revoke at will
An easement in gross that benefits a company, not a parcel
An easement by necessity giving a landlocked parcel access

explanation: An easement in gross benefits a person or company rather than a neighboring parcel, so there is a servient estate but no dominant estate. Commercial easements in gross held by utilities and pipelines are usually assignable. An easement appurtenant benefits a dominant parcel and runs with it, while a license is a revocable personal privilege.

distractorExplanations.a: An appurtenant easement needs a dominant parcel it benefits; here no neighboring land is benefited.
distractorExplanations.b: A recorded utility easement is a property interest, not a revocable permission.
distractorExplanations.d: An easement by necessity benefits a landlocked parcel, making it appurtenant rather than in gross.

prompt: Which list contains the protected classes under the federal Fair Housing Act?

options.text: Race, color, religion, sex, age, marital status, and national origin
Race, color, religion, sex, disability, source of income, and national origin
Race, color, religion, and national origin, with no other classes
Race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, and national origin

explanation: The federal Fair Housing Act protects seven classes: race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status (households with children under 18 and pregnant persons), and national origin. The Texas Fair Housing Act mirrors these classes. Age and marital status appear in other laws, such as ECOA for lending, but not in the federal Fair Housing Act.

distractorExplanations.a: Age and marital status are not federal Fair Housing Act classes; disability and familial status are.
distractorExplanations.b: Source of income is not a federal protected class, and this list leaves out familial status.
distractorExplanations.c: That list leaves out sex, disability, and familial status, which amendments added in 1974 and 1988.

prompt: A Texas seller is listing a house built in 1972. What does federal lead-based paint law require before the buyer is bound?

options.text: Known-hazard disclosure, the EPA pamphlet, and a chance to test
A lead inspection by a certified inspector before listing
Disclosure, if the seller actually knows there is lead
Nothing, because the rule covers commercial buildings

explanation: For target housing built before 1978, the seller must disclose any known lead-based paint and hazards and provide available reports, give the buyer the EPA pamphlet, include the required warning and disclosure form with the contract, and offer a 10-day opportunity to test, which the buyer may waive. Agents must ensure compliance.

distractorExplanations.b: The rule requires disclosure and a testing opportunity, not a mandatory inspection before listing.
distractorExplanations.c: The pamphlet, form, and testing opportunity are required for pre-1978 housing even if the seller knows of no lead.
distractorExplanations.d: The federal rule targets residential housing built before 1978, which includes this house.

prompt: A buyer's contract requires the seller to deliver marketable title. Which description fits marketable title?

options.text: Title free of every lien and easement, with no policy exceptions
Title free of significant defects that would deter a prudent buyer
Any title conveyed by general warranty deed, despite recorded defects
Title that a title company insured at some earlier sale

explanation: Marketable title is title a reasonable, prudent buyer would accept, free of significant defects or clouds that would expose the buyer to litigation or impair resale. Minor items such as standard utility easements and recorded subdivision restrictions usually do not make title unmarketable. Each sale requires a fresh title examination.

distractorExplanations.a: Marketable title can still carry minor exceptions; it must be free of defects that would deter a prudent buyer.
distractorExplanations.c: The deed type does not make title marketable; serious defects still make it unmarketable.
distractorExplanations.d: A past policy does not prove current marketability; title is examined again for each sale.

prompt: Luis leases retail space in Austin for his bakery and bolts commercial ovens and display cases to the floor. His lease ends next month, and the landlord says the equipment now belongs to the building. What is Luis's right?

options.text: The equipment became the landlord's once it was bolted down
He may remove it if the lease lists each item by name
He may remove it before the lease ends, repairing damage
He may remove it, but must pay the landlord its value

explanation: Equipment a tenant installs for a business is a trade fixture and stays the tenant's personal property even when bolted down. The tenant may remove it before the lease term ends but must repair damage caused by removal. Trade fixtures left behind after the tenancy ends may be treated as abandoned to the landlord.

distractorExplanations.a: Applies the ordinary fixture test (method of attachment) to a business tenant; trade fixtures stay the tenant's property despite bolting.
distractorExplanations.b: The trade fixture rule protects business tenants without an itemized clause; a lease may change it, but silence does not forfeit it.
distractorExplanations.d: Trade fixtures belong to the tenant, so removal requires no payment; the tenant owes repair of removal damage, not the item's value.

prompt: A seller plans to take the dining room chandelier, which is wired into the ceiling, but the TREC contract says nothing about it. What is the general rule?

options.text: She may take it, since light fixtures are personal property
She may take it if she installs one of similar value
She may take it, since unlisted items stay with the seller
It conveys as a fixture unless the contract excludes it

explanation: Items permanently attached to the home are fixtures and pass with the real property. The TREC One to Four Family contract's improvements paragraph lists attached items such as lighting fixtures and chandeliers as part of the sale. A seller who wants to keep one must exclude it in the contract or replace it before listing.

distractorExplanations.a: A wired-in chandelier is attached to the structure, so it is a fixture, not personal property.
distractorExplanations.b: A substitution needs the buyer's agreement in the contract; the seller cannot swap fixtures on her own.
distractorExplanations.c: Fixtures convey with the land by default; silence in the contract works against the seller here.

prompt: A homeowner in a deed-restricted Houston subdivision builds a carport the restrictions prohibit. Who typically enforces the restriction?

options.text: The HOA or other lot owners, through a civil lawsuit
The county appraisal district, through tax penalties
TREC, through discipline of the agent who sold the lot
The county clerk, who recorded the restrictions

explanation: Deed restrictions (restrictive covenants) are private land-use controls enforced by the parties they benefit, usually the property owners' association or other lot owners, through suits for an injunction or damages. They matter especially in Houston, which has no zoning ordinance and relies heavily on deed restrictions; the city can also help enforce certain restrictions.

distractorExplanations.b: Appraisal districts value property for taxes; they do not enforce private restrictions.
distractorExplanations.c: TREC regulates license holders; deed restrictions are enforced by the parties they benefit.
distractorExplanations.d: Recording gives notice; the clerk has no power to enforce what it records.

prompt: A Texas house is titled in the husband's name alone, but the couple lives there as their family homestead. Who must sign to sell it?

options.text: The husband, because his name is the one on the title
Both spouses, because selling a homestead needs both to join
The husband plus a probate judge who approves the homestead sale
The husband, if he first files a homestead release

explanation: Texas Family Code section 5.001 bars a spouse from selling, conveying, or encumbering the homestead without the joinder of the other spouse, whether the homestead is community or separate property and whether or not both names are on title. Title companies therefore require both spouses to sign the deed. Court involvement arises in limited cases, such as a spouse's incapacity.

distractorExplanations.a: Record title in one name does not override the homestead joinder rule; the other spouse must also sign.
distractorExplanations.c: Court approval is not routine; it applies in limited situations, such as a spouse's incapacity.
distractorExplanations.d: No unilateral release lets one spouse sell the family homestead without the other's joinder.

prompt: A survey ordered before closing shows the neighbor's garage extends two feet over the lot line onto the seller's land. What has the survey revealed?

options.text: An easement appurtenant created by the neighbor's garage
A mechanic's lien filed by the contractor who built the neighbor's garage
An encroachment of an improvement onto the seller's land
A lis pendens on the neighbor's pending lawsuit

explanation: An encroachment is an improvement, such as a building, fence, or driveway, that extends across a boundary onto another's land. Surveys reveal encroachments that title searches cannot, because they are physical rather than recorded. The buyer can object to it as a title or survey matter under the contract before closing.

distractorExplanations.a: A structure crossing the line is not an easement; an easement is a right of use, usually granted or created by law.
distractorExplanations.b: Liens are recorded claims found by a title search, not physical conditions shown on a survey.
distractorExplanations.d: A lis pendens is a recorded notice of litigation, not something a boundary survey reveals.

prompt: A Texas homeowner falls behind on several debts. Which creditor can generally force the sale of her homestead?

options.text: A credit card company holding a court judgment
A hospital owed money for unpaid medical bills
A personal lender holding an unsecured note
The lender holding the purchase-money deed of trust

explanation: The Texas Constitution protects a homestead from forced sale for most debts. Exceptions include purchase-money loans, property taxes, home equity and reverse mortgages that meet constitutional rules, properly contracted home-improvement liens, and certain owelty and refinance liens. Ordinary judgment creditors, medical providers, and unsecured lenders cannot force a sale.

distractorExplanations.a: A judgment for credit card debt cannot reach a Texas homestead; it is outside the constitutional exceptions.
distractorExplanations.b: Medical debt is unsecured and is not one of the debts allowed to force a homestead sale.
distractorExplanations.c: An unsecured note creates no lien on the homestead, so it cannot force a sale.

prompt: A family owns a home on one parcel inside Austin's city limits, served by city utilities. Under the Texas Property Code, what is the maximum acreage protected as their urban homestead?

options.text: 1 acre
5 acres
10 acres
200 acres

explanation: Texas Property Code section 41.002 protects an urban homestead of up to 10 acres in one or more contiguous lots, with improvements. A rural homestead may be up to 200 acres for a family or 100 acres for a single adult. Whether property is urban depends on factors such as city limits and the municipal services it receives.

distractorExplanations.a: One acre understates the protection; the current urban homestead cap is 10 acres.
distractorExplanations.b: Five acres understates the current urban limit of 10 acres.
distractorExplanations.d: 200 acres is the rural family homestead limit, not the urban limit.

prompt: A Texas homeowner has had the residence homestead exemption for several years. Market values in her area jump 25% in one year. By how much may her home's appraised value for tax purposes generally increase that year?

options.text: 0%, since value is frozen at the purchase price
Up to 3.5%
Up to 10%, plus new improvements
Up to 20%

explanation: Texas Tax Code section 23.23 caps the annual increase in a residence homestead's appraised value at 10% (plus the value of new improvements), starting the year after the owner qualifies. Market value can rise faster, but taxes are calculated on the capped value. A separate, temporary 20% cap has applied to certain non-homestead property under a value threshold.

distractorExplanations.a: Homestead values are not frozen at purchase; over-65 and disabled owners get school tax ceilings, a different benefit.
distractorExplanations.b: 3.5% relates to voter-approval tax rate limits for local governments, not the homestead appraisal cap.
distractorExplanations.d: 20% is the separate cap for certain non-homestead property, not the 10% homestead cap.

prompt: A seller conveys a Texas lot by special warranty deed. Years later a title defect created by an owner before the seller surfaces. What does the seller's deed warranty cover?

options.text: Defects from any time in the property's history
No warranties of any kind, like a quitclaim deed
Defects that the buyer's own title policy lists as exclusions
Defects arising during the seller's own ownership

explanation: A special warranty deed warrants title against defects arising by, through, or under the grantor, meaning during the seller's ownership. A general warranty deed warrants against defects from any time, and a quitclaim deed conveys whatever interest the grantor has with no warranty. The earlier owner's defect falls outside this seller's special warranty.

distractorExplanations.a: Warranting the whole chain of title describes a general warranty deed, not a special warranty deed.
distractorExplanations.b: A quitclaim gives no warranty; a special warranty deed still warrants against the grantor's own acts.
distractorExplanations.c: Title policy exclusions are separate from the seller's deed warranty and do not define its scope.

prompt: Buyer A receives a deed but does not record it. A week later the seller fraudulently deeds the same lot to Buyer B, who pays value, has no notice of A's deed, and records. Under Texas recording law, who generally prevails?

options.text: Buyer A, because her deed was delivered first
Buyer A, because recording is required for a valid deed
Neither, because the seller's fraud voids both deeds
Buyer B, as a later purchaser for value without notice

explanation: An unrecorded deed is valid between the seller and Buyer A, but the Texas recording statute makes it void as to a later purchaser for value without notice. Buyer B paid value, had no notice, and recorded, so B generally takes priority, and A's remedy is against the seller. Prompt recording protects buyers from this risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Being first in time does not protect an unrecorded deed against a later good-faith purchaser for value.
distractorExplanations.b: Recording is not needed for a deed to be valid between the parties; it protects against later purchasers.
distractorExplanations.c: The seller's fraud harms Buyer A, but it does not void the deed to an innocent purchaser for value.

prompt: A neighbor with no deed has openly fenced, used, and claimed a strip of rural land as his own, adversely and without interruption. Under Texas's general adverse possession statute for claimants without a title document, how long must he possess it?

options.text: 3 years
5 years
10 years
25 years

explanation: Texas has several adverse possession periods. The general 10-year statute applies to a claimant who peaceably and adversely cultivates, uses, or enjoys the land without any deed, subject to acreage limits. Shorter 3- and 5-year periods require title or color of title (and for 5 years, a recorded deed and paid taxes), and a 25-year statute covers special situations such as owners under a legal disability.

distractorExplanations.a: Three years requires title or color of title; this neighbor has no deed or title document.
distractorExplanations.b: Five years requires a recorded deed and payment of taxes, which this claimant lacks.
distractorExplanations.d: Twenty-five years covers special situations; the general period for a claimant without a deed is ten years.

prompt: A Hill Country landowner drills a well and pumps groundwater for irrigation, lowering a neighbor's well. What doctrine generally governs his right to that groundwater in Texas?

options.text: The rule of capture, subject to groundwater district rules
Riparian rights, sharing reasonable use with adjoining owners
Prior appropriation, giving the first permit holder priority
State ownership, requiring a TCEQ permit for every well

explanation: Texas landowners own the groundwater beneath their land, and under the rule of capture they may generally pump it even if a neighbor's well is affected, absent malice or waste. Local groundwater conservation districts can regulate spacing and production. Surface water, by contrast, is state-owned and allocated by TCEQ permits under prior appropriation.

distractorExplanations.b: Riparian rights concern surface water along streams, not groundwater pumped from a well.
distractorExplanations.c: Prior appropriation and TCEQ permits govern Texas surface water, not groundwater.
distractorExplanations.d: Texas groundwater belongs to the landowner; TCEQ permits are for surface water.

prompt: A seller's deed reserves all oil, gas, and other minerals. The buyer later learns a company holding a lease from the seller plans to drill on the property. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The buyer can block drilling because she owns the surface
The mineral estate is dominant and may reasonably use the surface
The reservation is void because minerals cannot be severed
The buyer receives the royalties because she owns the land

explanation: In Texas, minerals can be severed from the surface by a reservation in a deed, creating separate estates. The mineral estate is dominant, so the mineral owner or lessee may make reasonable use of the surface to develop minerals, subject to the accommodation doctrine. Buyers should check deeds and the title commitment for mineral reservations.

distractorExplanations.a: Surface ownership does not let the buyer bar reasonable mineral development by the dominant mineral estate.
distractorExplanations.c: Texas routinely allows minerals to be severed by reservation or separate conveyance.
distractorExplanations.d: Royalties go to the owner of the mineral estate, which the seller kept by reservation.

prompt: A Texas tenant moves out, surrenders the unit, and gives the landlord a forwarding address. Under the Texas Property Code, how long does the landlord generally have to refund the security deposit or itemize deductions?

options.text: 10 days
30 days
45 days
60 days

explanation: Texas Property Code chapter 92 requires a residential landlord to refund the security deposit, with a written itemized list of any deductions, within 30 days after the tenant surrenders the premises. The landlord need not act until the tenant gives a forwarding address, and a bad-faith failure exposes the landlord to added statutory penalties.

distractorExplanations.a: Ten days is far shorter than the Texas residential deadline of 30 days.
distractorExplanations.c: Forty-five days is used in some other states; Texas sets 30 days after surrender.
distractorExplanations.d: Sixty days is twice the Texas residential deadline.

prompt: A sales agent shows a Hispanic couple homes in mostly Hispanic neighborhoods, though they asked to see homes across the city. What fair housing violation is this?

options.text: Steering buyers toward areas based on national origin
Blockbusting, inducing sales by citing who is moving in
Redlining, refusing loans in certain neighborhoods
Discriminatory advertising of a housing preference

explanation: Steering is directing buyers or renters toward or away from areas based on a protected class, here national origin. It violates the federal and Texas Fair Housing Acts even if the couple never complains. Agents should show homes that match the buyer's stated criteria, such as price, size, and location, not assumptions about who belongs where.

distractorExplanations.b: Blockbusting means urging owners to sell by claiming a protected group is moving in; no one was induced to sell here.
distractorExplanations.c: Redlining is refusing or limiting loans or insurance in certain areas; this agent controlled showings, not credit.
distractorExplanations.d: No ad expressed a preference; the violation occurred in the showings themselves.

prompt: A Texas apartment complex has a no-pets policy. A tenant with a disability provides reliable documentation that she needs an assistance animal. What must the landlord generally do?

options.text: Refuse, because the no-pets policy applies to every tenant
Allow the animal but charge the standard pet deposit
Allow it if the animal is certified as a trained service dog
Allow it as a reasonable accommodation, without pet fees

explanation: Under the Fair Housing Act, refusing a reasonable accommodation in rules or policies that a person with a disability needs is discrimination. An assistance animal, including an emotional support animal, is not a pet, so absent a direct threat or undue burden the landlord must waive the no-pets rule and may not charge pet deposits or fees; the tenant remains liable for actual damage.

distractorExplanations.a: A blanket no-pets policy must yield to a reasonable accommodation for a person with a disability.
distractorExplanations.b: Pet deposits and fees cannot be charged for an assistance animal, though the tenant is liable for actual damage.
distractorExplanations.c: Assistance animals under the Fair Housing Act include support animals; no certification or training is required.

prompt: A suburban Houston home lies within a municipal utility district (MUD) that levies its own tax to repay bonds. What does Texas law require of the seller?

options.text: Paying off the district's bonds before closing
Obtaining the district's approval of the buyer
Giving the buyer the statutory MUD notice
Escrowing two years of district taxes at closing

explanation: Texas Water Code section 49.452 requires the seller of property in a MUD or similar district to give the buyer a statutory notice describing the district, its tax rate, and its bonded debt, ideally before the contract is signed. If the notice is not given in time, the buyer may have the right to terminate. The TREC contract refers to this notice.

distractorExplanations.a: District bonds are repaid over time through district taxes; the seller does not retire them at sale.
distractorExplanations.b: Districts do not approve buyers; the seller's duty is to give the statutory notice.
distractorExplanations.d: No rule requires escrowing district taxes beyond normal prorations; the requirement is disclosure.

prompt: A seller has a survey from her purchase eight years ago, and nothing has been built since. The TREC contract lets her furnish an existing survey. What does she usually sign so the title company can accept it?

options.text: A T-47 residential real property affidavit
An amended seller's disclosure notice
A Non-Realty Items Addendum
A Notice of Buyer's Termination of Contract

explanation: In Texas, a seller furnishing an existing survey typically signs a T-47 Residential Real Property Affidavit (or the newer T-47.1 declaration), a Texas Department of Insurance form stating that no changes such as new improvements or boundary fences have occurred. If the title company accepts it, coverage can issue without a new survey; otherwise a new survey may be required under the contract.

distractorExplanations.b: The disclosure notice reports condition; it is not the title company's affidavit about the survey.
distractorExplanations.c: That addendum covers personal property sold with the house, not surveys.
distractorExplanations.d: A termination notice ends the contract; it has nothing to do with accepting an existing survey.

prompt: An appraiser must value a 40-year-old church that rarely sells and produces no rental income. Which approach is usually most relevant?

options.text: The sales comparison approach
The cost approach
The income capitalization approach
The gross rent multiplier method

explanation: The cost approach estimates value as land value plus the current cost to build the improvements, minus depreciation. It is most useful for special-purpose properties such as churches, schools, and fire stations, which rarely sell and produce no rent, leaving too few comparables for the sales approach and no income for the income approach.

distractorExplanations.a: Sales comparison needs recent comparable sales, which are scarce for special-purpose buildings.
distractorExplanations.c: Income capitalization needs rental income; this church produces none.
distractorExplanations.d: A gross rent multiplier applies to rental properties, and this church earns no rent.

prompt: A homeowner's odd-shaped lot makes it impossible to meet the city's 25-foot front setback for a modest addition. What should she request from the zoning board?

options.text: A rezoning of the entire neighborhood
A nonconforming use designation
A conditional use permit for her home
A variance from the setback requirement

explanation: A variance grants relief from a specific zoning requirement, such as a setback or height limit, when strict application causes unnecessary hardship due to unique conditions of the property, like an odd lot shape. Rezoning changes a district's rules, a nonconforming use is a pre-existing use allowed to continue, and a conditional use permit allows a special use.

distractorExplanations.a: Rezoning changes the rules for an area; she needs relief for one lot from one requirement.
distractorExplanations.b: Nonconforming (grandfathered) status protects a use that existed before the zoning; it does not authorize new construction.
distractorExplanations.c: A conditional use permit allows a special use in a zone; her residential use is already permitted.
